title: Kinetic Theory of Gases (KTG)
subtitle: Zero-to-JEE-Advanced Visual Textbook: Postulates of KTG, Ideal Gas Laws, Microscopic Pressure Derivation, RMS/Average/Most Probable Speeds, Maxwell Distribution, Degrees of Freedom, Equipartition of Energy, Mean Free Path & Real Gases
introduction:
💡 First-Time Reader Intuition: Connecting Invisible Atoms to Macroscopic Pressure & Temperature

In Chapter 11 (Thermodynamics), we treated a gas as a continuous fluid described by macroscopic variables like Pressure ($P$), Volume ($V$), and Temperature ($T$). We never asked why a gas exerts pressure on the walls of a balloon or what temperature actually looks like at the atomic scale.

Kinetic Theory of Gases (KTG) zooms in with a microscopic lens: a gas is a swarm of trillions of tiny molecules flying around at high speeds ($\sim 500\text{ m/s}$) in complete chaos. Every time a molecule bounces off the container wall, it delivers a tiny momentum kick. The sum of trillions of such collisions per second is what we feel as steady Gas Pressure ($P$), and the average translational kinetic energy of each molecule is what our thermometer reads as Absolute Temperature ($T$)!

The 5 Fundamental Postulates of an Ideal Gas in KTG:
  • 1. Point-Mass Molecules: The actual volume of the gas molecules themselves is negligible compared to the total volume $V$ of the container.
  • 2. Zero Intermolecular Forces: Molecules exert no attractive or repulsive forces on one another except during the brief instant of collision (hence internal potential energy $U_{\text{potential}} = 0$).
  • 3. Perfectly Elastic Collisions: All molecule-molecule and molecule-wall collisions are perfectly elastic ($e = 1$); total kinetic energy is strictly conserved.
  • 4. Isotropic Random Motion: Molecules move randomly in all directions with equal probability, so average velocity components are symmetric: $\langle v_x^2 \rangle = \langle v_y^2 \rangle = \langle v_z^2 \rangle = \frac{1}{3}\langle v^2 \rangle$.
  • 5. Instantaneous Impact: The duration of a collision is negligible compared to the time spent traveling freely between collisions.

topics.title: Ideal Gas Equation, Classical Gas Laws, Dalton's Partial Pressure Law & Microscopic Pressure Formula
topics.theoryHtml:
1.1 The Ideal Gas Equation in All 4 Standard Forms
Universal Gas Constant ($R$) vs. Boltzmann Constant ($k_B$):
• $R = 8.314\text{ J mol}^{-1}\text{ K}^{-1} \approx \frac{25}{3}\text{ J mol}^{-1}\text{ K}^{-1} \approx 2\text{ cal mol}^{-1}\text{ K}^{-1}$ (used when counting in moles $n$).
• $k_B = \frac{R}{N_A} = 1.38 \times 10^{-23}\text{ J K}^{-1}$ (used when counting individual molecules $N$, where $N_A = 6.022 \times 10^{23}\text{ mol}^{-1}$).
$$\begin{aligned} \text{1. Mole Form:} & \quad \boxed{P V = n R T} \qquad \left(\text{where } n = \frac{\text{Mass }(m_{\text{total}})}{\text{Molar Mass }(M)} = \frac{N}{N_A}\right) \\[6pt] \text{2. Molecule Form:} & \quad \boxed{P V = N k_B T} \qquad \bigg| \qquad \text{Number Density } \left(n_v = \frac{N}{V}\right): \quad \boxed{P = n_v k_B T} \\[6pt] \text{3. Density Form:} & \quad \boxed{P = \frac{\rho R T}{M} = \frac{\rho k_B T}{m_0}} \qquad (m_0 = \text{mass of 1 molecule}, \; M = \text{molar mass in kg/mol}) \end{aligned}$$
Gas LawCondition Held ConstantMathematical Relation
1. Boyle's LawConstant $T$ and $n$$P \propto \frac{1}{V} \implies P_1 V_1 = P_2 V_2 = \text{Constant}$
2. Charles's LawConstant $P$ and $n$$V \propto T \implies \frac{V_1}{T_1} = \frac{V_2}{T_2}$ ($T$ in Kelvin!)
3. Gay-Lussac's LawConstant $V$ and $n$$P \propto T \implies \frac{P_1}{T_1} = \frac{P_2}{T_2}$
4. Avogadro's LawSame $P, V,$ and $T$Equal volumes of all ideal gases contain equal numbers of molecules ($N_1 = N_2$).
5. Dalton's Law of Partial PressuresNon-reacting gas mixture in volume $V$ at $T$$$P_{\text{total}} = P_1 + P_2 + \dots = (n_1 + n_2 + \dots)\frac{RT}{V}$$
1.2 Microscopic Pressure Exerted by an Ideal Gas

Consider $N$ molecules, each of mass $m_0$ (total gas mass $M_{\text{gas}} = N m_0$, density $\rho = \frac{N m_0}{V}$), moving inside a container of volume $V$ with root-mean-square speed $v_{\text{rms}} = \sqrt{\langle v^2 \rangle}$:

$$\boxed{P = \frac{1}{3}\frac{N m_0}{V}\langle v^2 \rangle = \frac{1}{3}\rho v_{\text{rms}}^2 = \frac{2}{3}\left(\frac{E_{\text{trans}}}{V}\right)}$$

Notice the fundamental relation: Pressure of an ideal gas is always equal to two-thirds ($\frac{2}{3}$) of its translational kinetic energy per unit volume!
topics.derivationHtml:
Complete First-Principles Derivation of Gas Pressure P = (1/3) ρ v_rms²

Consider a cubical box of side length $L$ (volume $V = L^3$) containing $N$ gas molecules, each of mass $m_0$.

Step 1 (Momentum imparted in 1 collision with right wall $x = L$): A molecule with velocity $(v_x, v_y, v_z)$ hits the wall perpendicular to the $x$-axis and rebounds elastically with $(-v_x, v_y, v_z)$. Momentum imparted to the wall is $\Delta p_x = 2 m_0 v_x$.

Step 2 (Time between successive collisions with the same wall): The molecule must travel to the opposite wall ($L$) and back ($L$), covering distance $2L$ at speed $v_x$, so $\Delta t = \frac{2L}{v_x}$.

Step 3 (Force and Pressure from all $N$ molecules): Force exerted by the $i^{\text{th}}$ molecule is $f_i = \frac{\Delta p_x}{\Delta t} = \frac{2m_0 v_{xi}}{2L / v_{xi}} = \frac{m_0 v_{xi}^2}{L}$. Summing over all $N$ molecules and dividing by wall area $A = L^2$ (using $L^3 = V$):

$$P = \frac{\sum f_i}{L^2} = \frac{m_0}{L^3}\sum_{i=1}^N v_{xi}^2 = \frac{N m_0}{V}\langle v_x^2 \rangle$$

Step 4 (Isotropy in 3D space): Since $\langle v^2 \rangle = \langle v_x^2 \rangle + \langle v_y^2 \rangle + \langle v_z^2 \rangle$ and all three directions are equivalent ($\langle v_x^2 \rangle = \langle v_y^2 \rangle = \langle v_z^2 \rangle = \frac{1}{3}\langle v^2 \rangle$):

$$\boxed{P = \frac{1}{3}\frac{N m_0}{V}\langle v^2 \rangle = \frac{1}{3}\rho v_{\text{rms}}^2}$$

topics.jeeTraps:
• Trap 1 (Slope of $V$-$T$ vs. $P$-$T$ Graphs): On a $V$ vs. $T$ graph ($V = \left(\frac{nR}{P}\right)T$), the slope is inversely proportional to pressure $P$, so a steeper line corresponds to a lower pressure ($P_1 < P_2$)! Conversely, if $T$ is plotted on the y-axis and $V$ on the x-axis ($T = \left(\frac{P}{nR}\right)V$), a steeper line has higher pressure! Always check which variable is on which axis.
  • Trap 2 (Does Gas Pressure Depend on Container Shape?): Although we derived $P = \frac{1}{3}\rho v_{\text{rms}}^2$ using a cube, the result is valid for a container of any arbitrary shape (sphere, cylinder, irregular vessel).

topics.title: Molecular Speeds (RMS, Average & Most Probable), Maxwell Speed Distribution & Translational Kinetic Energy
topics.theoryHtml:
2.1 The 3 Characteristic Molecular Speeds ($v_{\text{mp}} < v_{\text{avg}} < v_{\text{rms}}$)

Because gas molecules constantly collide, they do not all move at the same speed. We characterize their speed distribution using three standard averages (where $M$ is molar mass in $\text{kg/mol}$ and $m_0$ is the mass of one molecule in $\text{kg}$):

Speed NameDefinitionMaster FormulaNumerical Factor
1. Most Probable Speed ($v_{\text{mp}}$)Speed possessed by the maximum fraction of molecules (peak of Maxwell curve).$$\boxed{v_{\text{mp}} = \sqrt{\frac{2RT}{M}} = \sqrt{\frac{2k_B T}{m_0}} = \sqrt{\frac{2P}{\rho}}}$$$\sqrt{2} \approx 1.414$
2. Average (Mean) Speed ($v_{\text{avg}}$)Arithmetic mean of speeds: $\frac{v_1 + v_2 + \dots + v_N}{N}$.$$\boxed{v_{\text{avg}} = \sqrt{\frac{8RT}{\pi M}} = \sqrt{\frac{8k_B T}{\pi m_0}} = \sqrt{\frac{8P}{\pi\rho}}}$$$\sqrt{\frac{8}{\pi}} \approx 1.596$
3. Root-Mean-Square Speed ($v_{\text{rms}}$)Square root of the mean of squared speeds: $\sqrt{\frac{v_1^2 + v_2^2 + \dots + v_N^2}{N}}$.$$\boxed{v_{\text{rms}} = \sqrt{\frac{3RT}{M}} = \sqrt{\frac{3k_B T}{m_0}} = \sqrt{\frac{3P}{\rho}}}$$$\sqrt{3} \approx 1.732$
$$\textbf{Ratio to Memorize:} \quad \boxed{v_{\text{mp}} : v_{\text{avg}} : v_{\text{rms}} = \sqrt{2} : \sqrt{\frac{8}{\pi}} : \sqrt{3} = 1 : 1.128 : 1.224} \qquad \left(\text{Speed of Sound: } v_s = \sqrt{\frac{\gamma RT}{M}} = \sqrt{\frac{\gamma}{3}}\,v_{\text{rms}}\right)$$
2.2 Translational Kinetic Energy of an Ideal Gas
$$\text{1. Average Translational KE of 1 Molecule:} \quad \boxed{\langle K_{\text{trans}} \rangle = \frac{1}{2}m_0 v_{\text{rms}}^2 = \frac{3}{2}k_B T}$$
$$\text{2. Total Translational KE of } n \text{ Moles:} \quad \boxed{E_{\text{trans}} = \frac{3}{2}n R T = \frac{3}{2}P V}$$
Crucial Physical Insight:
At the same temperature $T = 300\text{ K}$, a light Helium atom ($M = 4\text{ g/mol}$) and a heavy Oxygen molecule ($M = 32\text{ g/mol}$) have the exact same average translational kinetic energy ($\frac{3}{2}k_B T$), even though the Helium atom moves $\sqrt{32/4} = 2\sqrt{2}$ times faster!
topics.derivationHtml:
Maxwell-Boltzmann Speed Distribution Function & Proof of v_mp = √(2k_B T / m₀)

James Clerk Maxwell proved that the number of molecules $dN$ having speeds between $v$ and $v + dv$ is given by:

$$\frac{dN}{dv} = f(v) = 4\pi N \left(\frac{m_0}{2\pi k_B T}\right)^{3/2} v^2 e^{-\frac{m_0 v^2}{2k_B T}}$$

To find the Most Probable Speed ($v_{\text{mp}}$) where the distribution curve reaches its maximum peak, set $\frac{d}{dv}\left(v^2 e^{-\alpha v^2}\right) = 0$ (where $\alpha = \frac{m_0}{2k_B T}$):

$$2v e^{-\alpha v^2} + v^2(-2\alpha v)e^{-\alpha v^2} = 0 \implies 1 - \alpha v_{\text{mp}}^2 = 0 \implies v_{\text{mp}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\alpha}} = \boxed{\sqrt{\frac{2k_B T}{m_0}}}$$

topics.jeeTraps:
• Trap 1 (Putting Molar Mass $M$ in Grams Instead of Kilograms!): In $v_{\text{rms}} = \sqrt{\frac{3RT}{M}}$, SI units require $M$ in $\text{kg/mol}$! For Oxygen ($\text{O}_2$, molecular weight $32$), you MUST substitute $M = 32 \times 10^{-3}\text{ kg/mol}$ (NOT $32$)!
  • Trap 2 (Does Increasing Pressure at Constant Temperature Increase $v_{\text{rms}}$?): Students look at $v_{\text{rms}} = \sqrt{3P/\rho}$ and think doubling $P$ increases $v_{\text{rms}}$. WRONG! At constant temperature $T$, doubling $P$ also doubles the density $\rho$, so the ratio $P/\rho = RT/M$ remains constant and $v_{\text{rms}}$ does NOT change!

topics.title: Degrees of Freedom, Law of Equipartition of Energy, Specific Heats (Cv, Cp, γ) & Gas Mixtures

prerequisites.label: First Law of Thermodynamics & Mayer's Relation

topics.theoryHtml:
3.1 Degrees of Freedom ($f$) & Law of Equipartition of Energy
Definition (Degrees of Freedom $f$):
The total number of independent coordinates or independent squared velocity/displacement terms required to completely specify the dynamical state (configuration and energy) of a molecule: $$f = f_{\text{translational}} + f_{\text{rotational}} + 2 f_{\text{vibrational modes}}$$
Law of Equipartition of Energy (Maxwell):
For any dynamical system in thermal equilibrium at absolute temperature $T$, the total internal energy is distributed equally among all degrees of freedom, and the energy associated with each molecule per degree of freedom is $\frac{1}{2}k_B T$ (or $\frac{1}{2}RT$ per mole).
Gas Type & ExamplesTrans.Rot.Total $f$$C_V = \frac{f}{2}R$$C_P = \left(\frac{f}{2}+1\right)R$$\gamma = 1 + \frac{2}{f}$
1. Monoatomic ($\text{He, Ne, Ar}$)$3$$0$$\mathbf{3}$$\frac{3}{2}R$$\frac{5}{2}R$$\frac{5}{3} = 1.67$
2. Diatomic (Rigid, Room $T$) ($\text{H}_2, \text{O}_2, \text{N}_2$)$3$$2$$\mathbf{5}$$\frac{5}{2}R$$\frac{7}{2}R$$\frac{7}{5} = 1.40$
3. Diatomic (High $T$, with Vibration)$3$$2$ (+2 vib)$\mathbf{7}$$\frac{7}{2}R$$\frac{9}{2}R$$\frac{9}{7} \approx 1.29$
4. Linear Polyatomic ($\text{CO}_2, \text{C}_2\text{H}_2$, room $T$)$3$$2$$\mathbf{5}$$\frac{5}{2}R$$\frac{7}{2}R$$\frac{7}{5} = 1.40$
5. Non-Linear Polyatomic ($\text{H}_2\text{O, NH}_3, \text{CH}_4$)$3$$3$$\mathbf{6}$$3R$$4R$$\frac{4}{3} = 1.33$
3.2 Mixing of Two Non-Reacting Ideal Gases (Very High Yield in JEE!)

Suppose $n_1$ moles of Gas 1 ($f_1, C_{V1}, T_1$) and $n_2$ moles of Gas 2 ($f_2, C_{V2}, T_2$) are mixed in an insulated container:

$$\text{1. Equilibrium Mixture Temperature:} \quad U_i = U_f \implies \boxed{T_{\text{mix}} = \frac{n_1 f_1 T_1 + n_2 f_2 T_2}{n_1 f_1 + n_2 f_2} = \frac{n_1 C_{V1} T_1 + n_2 C_{V2} T_2}{n_1 C_{V1} + n_2 C_{V2}}}$$
$$\text{2. Mixture } C_V, C_P, \text{ and } \gamma_{\text{mix}}: \quad \boxed{C_{V,\text{mix}} = \frac{n_1 C_{V1} + n_2 C_{V2}}{n_1 + n_2}}, \qquad \boxed{\gamma_{\text{mix}} = \frac{n_1 C_{P1} + n_2 C_{P2}}{n_1 C_{V1} + n_2 C_{V2}}}$$
topics.derivationHtml:
Why 1 Vibrational Mode Adds 2 Degrees of Freedom & Dulong-Petit Law for Solids

1. Vibrational Mode ($+2$ to $f$): A vibrating bond behaves like a 1D harmonic oscillator with total energy $E_{\text{vib}} = \frac{1}{2}\mu v_r^2 + \frac{1}{2}kx^2$. Because it contains two quadratic terms (kinetic energy + spring potential energy), Equipartition assigns $\frac{1}{2}k_B T + \frac{1}{2}k_B T = 1\,k_B T$ per vibrational mode (equivalent to $2$ degrees of freedom)!

2. Dulong-Petit Law for Crystalline Solids: Each atom in a 3D crystal lattice vibrates along $x, y,$ and $z$ ($3$ independent vibrational modes $= 3 \times 2 = 6$ degrees of freedom). Thus internal energy per mole is $U = 6 \times \frac{1}{2}RT = 3RT$, giving molar heat capacity:

$$\boxed{C_V = \frac{dU}{dT} = 3R \approx 24.94\text{ J mol}^{-1}\text{ K}^{-1}}$$

topics.jeeTraps:
• Trap 1 (Never Average $\gamma_1$ and $\gamma_2$ Directly as $\frac{n_1\gamma_1 + n_2\gamma_2}{n_1 + n_2}$!): Because $\gamma = C_P/C_V$ is a ratio of heat capacities, $\gamma_{\text{mix}}$ is NOT the weighted average of $\gamma_1$ and $\gamma_2$! You must ALWAYS compute $\gamma_{\text{mix}} = \frac{n_1 C_{P1} + n_2 C_{P2}}{n_1 C_{V1} + n_2 C_{V2}}$ (or use $\frac{n_1 + n_2}{\gamma_{\text{mix}} - 1} = \frac{n_1}{\gamma_1 - 1} + \frac{n_2}{\gamma_2 - 1}$)!
  • Trap 2 (Translational KE vs. Total Internal Energy of a Diatomic Gas): For a diatomic gas ($f = 5$), total internal energy is $U = \frac{5}{2}nRT$ ($\frac{3}{2}nRT$ translational $+ \frac{2}{2}nRT$ rotational). If the question specifically asks for Translational Kinetic Energy, the answer is STILL $\mathbf{\frac{3}{2}nRT}$ (NOT $\frac{5}{2}nRT$)!

topics.title: Mean Free Path (λ), Collision Frequency & Van der Waals Equation of State for Real Gases
topics.theoryHtml:
4.1 Mean Free Path ($\lambda$) & Collision Frequency ($f_c$)
Definition (Mean Free Path $\lambda$):
The average distance traveled by a gas molecule between two successive collisions with other molecules. If $d$ is the diameter of each spherical molecule and $n_v = \frac{N}{V} = \frac{P}{k_B T}$ is the number of molecules per unit volume:
$$\boxed{\lambda = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}\,\pi n_v d^2} = \frac{k_B T}{\sqrt{2}\,\pi d^2 P} = \frac{m_0}{\sqrt{2}\,\pi d^2 \rho}}$$
$$\text{Relaxation Time (Mean Time Between Collisions):} \quad \tau = \frac{\lambda}{v_{\text{avg}}} \qquad \bigg| \qquad \text{Collision Frequency:} \quad f_c = \frac{1}{\tau} = \frac{v_{\text{avg}}}{\lambda}$$

How $\lambda$ Depends on $T$ and $P$:
• At constant volume (or constant density $\rho$), $n_v$ is constant, so $\lambda$ is independent of temperature and pressure!
• At constant pressure $P$, $\lambda \propto T$. At constant temperature $T$, $\lambda \propto \frac{1}{P}$.

4.2 Real Gases & Van der Waals Equation of State

Real gases deviate from $PV = nRT$ at high pressures and low temperatures because two ideal assumptions break down: (1) finite molecular size reduces free volume by $nb$, and (2) intermolecular attractions reduce wall impact pressure by $\frac{an^2}{V^2}$:

$$\boxed{\left(P + \frac{a n^2}{V^2}\right)(V - n b) = n R T}$$
  • Constant $a$ (Intermolecular Attraction): SI unit $= \text{Pa}\cdot\text{m}^6\text{ mol}^{-2} = \text{N}\cdot\text{m}^4\text{ mol}^{-2}$; Dimensions $= [M^1 L^5 T^{-2}\text{mol}^{-2}]$.
  • Constant $b$ (Excluded Volume per Mole): Equal to $4 \times$ the actual volume of 1 mole of molecules ($b = 4 N_A \left(\frac{4}{3}\pi r^3\right)$). SI unit $= \text{m}^3\text{ mol}^{-1}$; Dimensions $= [M^0 L^3 T^0\text{mol}^{-1}]$.
  • Critical Temperature ($T_c$): The highest temperature at which a gas can be liquefied by pressure alone: $T_c = \frac{8a}{27Rb}$.
topics.derivationHtml:
Geometric Cylinder-Sweep Derivation of Mean Free Path λ = 1 / (√2 π n_v d²)

Imagine one molecule of diameter $d$ moving at speed $v$ for time $t$, while other molecules are momentarily frozen. Any other molecule whose center lies inside a cylinder of radius $d$ (cross-sectional collision area $\sigma = \pi d^2$) and length $vt$ will collide with it!

Step 1: Number of molecules inside this swept cylinder is $N_{\text{coll}} = n_v (\pi d^2 v t)$.

Step 2: When all molecules are moving, replace $v$ with the mean relative speed between two molecules $\langle v_{\text{rel}} \rangle = \sqrt{2}\,v$. Dividing total distance $vt$ by number of collisions $N_{\text{coll}}$ gives:

$$\boxed{\lambda = \frac{\text{Distance Traveled}}{\text{Number of Collisions}} = \frac{v t}{\sqrt{2}\,n_v \pi d^2 v t} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}\,\pi n_v d^2}}$$

topics.jeeTraps: • Trap (Mean Free Path in a Sealed Rigid Container When Heated): If a gas is sealed in a rigid container ($V = \text{constant}$, $N = \text{constant}$) and heated from $300\text{ K}$ to $600\text{ K}$, students use $\lambda = \frac{k_B T}{\sqrt{2}\pi d^2 P}$ and think $\lambda$ doubles! WRONG! In a rigid vessel, $P$ also doubles when $T$ doubles, so $n_v = N/V = P/(k_B T)$ remains constant, and $\lambda$ does NOT change at all! (However, collision frequency $f_c = v_{\text{avg}}/\lambda \propto \sqrt{T}$ increases by $\sqrt{2}$).

conclusion: You have mastered Chapter 12: Kinetic Theory of Gases! With microscopic pressure, Maxwell speeds, Equipartition of Energy, gas mixture laws, and Mean Free Path under your belt, you have completed the entire Heat & Thermodynamics unit of Class 11 Physics.
summary:
• Gas Pressure & KE: $P = \frac{1}{3}\rho v_{\text{rms}}^2 = \frac{2}{3}(E_{\text{trans}}/V)$; $E_{\text{trans}} = \frac{3}{2}nRT = \frac{3}{2}PV$.
  • Molecular Speeds: $v_{\text{mp}} = \sqrt{\frac{2RT}{M}} < v_{\text{avg}} = \sqrt{\frac{8RT}{\pi M}} < v_{\text{rms}} = \sqrt{\frac{3RT}{M}}$.
  • Equipartition: Each degree of freedom has $\frac{1}{2}k_B T$ per molecule; $U = \frac{f}{2}nRT$, $C_V = \frac{f}{2}R$, $C_P = \left(\frac{f}{2}+1\right)R$, $\gamma = 1 + \frac{2}{f}$.
  • Mean Free Path: $\lambda = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}\pi n_v d^2} = \frac{k_B T}{\sqrt{2}\pi d^2 P}$.

ConceptMaster FormulaKey Notes
Microscopic Pressure$P = \dfrac{1}{3}\rho v_{\text{rms}}^2 = \dfrac{2}{3}\left(\dfrac{E_{\text{trans}}}{V}\right)$Translational KE per mole $= \dfrac{3}{2}RT$ for ALL gases.
3 Molecular Speeds$v_{\text{mp}} : v_{\text{avg}} : v_{\text{rms}} = \sqrt{2} : \sqrt{\dfrac{8}{\pi}} : \sqrt{3}$$M$ in $\sqrt{3RT/M}$ must be in $\text{kg/mol}$!
Equipartition & $\gamma$$C_V = \dfrac{f}{2}R, \quad C_P = \left(\dfrac{f}{2}+1\right)R, \quad \gamma = 1 + \dfrac{2}{f}$Mono: $f=3$; Dia: $f=5$; Non-linear poly: $f=6$.
Adiabatic Index of Mixture$\gamma_{\text{mix}} = \dfrac{n_1 C_{P1} + n_2 C_{P2}}{n_1 C_{V1} + n_2 C_{V2}}$Never average $\gamma_1$ and $\gamma_2$ directly!
Mean Free Path$\lambda = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}\pi n_v d^2} = \dfrac{k_B T}{\sqrt{2}\pi d^2 P}$Constant in a rigid sealed container ($n_v = \text{const}$).

questions.prompt: At what temperature will the root-mean-square ($v_{\text{rms}}$) speed of Oxygen ($\text{O}_2$, molar mass $32\text{ g/mol}$) molecules be equal to the $v_{\text{rms}}$ speed of Hydrogen ($\text{H}_2$, molar mass $2\text{ g/mol}$) molecules at $T_{\text{H}_2} = 100\text{ K}$?

What is the ratio of the average translational kinetic energy of a Helium atom ($M = 4\text{ g/mol}$) to that of an Nitrogen molecule ($M = 28\text{ g/mol}$) both kept at the same temperature of $300\text{ K}$?
questions.explanation: Average translational kinetic energy of ANY gas molecule depends ONLY on absolute temperature: $\langle K_{\text{trans}} \rangle = \frac{3}{2}k_B T$. Since both gases are at $300\text{ K}$, the ratio is strictly $1 : 1$!

questions.prompt: A gaseous mixture consists of $2\text{ moles}$ of Oxygen ($\text{O}_2$, diatomic, $f = 5$) and $4\text{ moles}$ of Argon ($\text{Ar}$, monoatomic, $f = 3$) at temperature $T$. Neglecting all vibrational modes, the total internal energy $U$ of the mixture is:
If $1\text{ mole}$ of a monoatomic gas ($\gamma = 5/3$) is mixed with $1\text{ mole}$ of a diatomic gas ($\gamma = 7/5$), the value of the adiabatic exponent $\gamma_{\text{mix}}$ for the mixture is:
questions.explanation: For monoatomic: $C_{V1} = \frac{3}{2}R, C_{P1} = \frac{5}{2}R$. For diatomic: $C_{V2} = \frac{5}{2}R, C_{P2} = \frac{7}{2}R$. Using $\gamma_{\text{mix}} = \frac{n_1 C_{P1} + n_2 C_{P2}}{n_1 C_{V1} + n_2 C_{V2}} = \frac{\frac{5}{2}R + \frac{7}{2}R}{\frac{3}{2}R + \frac{5}{2}R} = \frac{6R}{4R} = \frac{3}{2} = 1.50$.

questions.prompt: The mean free path $\lambda$ of molecules of a gas of molecular radius $r$ is inversely proportional to:
questions.explanation: Since molecular diameter is $d = 2r$, the mean free path formula $\lambda = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}\pi n_v d^2} = \frac{1}{4\sqrt{2}\pi n_v r^2}$ shows that $\lambda \propto \frac{1}{r^2}$.

questions.prompt: An insulated container is divided into two compartments. One compartment contains $n_1 = 2\text{ moles}$ of Helium ($f_1 = 3$) at temperature $T_1 = 300\text{ K}$, and the other contains $n_2 = 1\text{ mole}$ of Oxygen ($f_2 = 5$) at temperature $T_2 = 630\text{ K}$. If the partition is removed so the gases mix without doing any external work, what is the final equilibrium temperature $T_{\text{mix}}$?
questions.explanation: Since the container is insulated and rigid ($Q = 0, W = 0$), total internal energy is conserved ($\Delta U_1 + \Delta U_2 = 0$): $T_{\text{mix}} = \frac{n_1 f_1 T_1 + n_2 f_2 T_2}{n_1 f_1 + n_2 f_2} = \frac{2(3)(300) + 1(5)(630)}{2(3) + 1(5)} = \frac{1800 + 3150}{6 + 5} = \frac{4950}{11} = 450\text{ K}$.
